rows.question: The life of a building permit and of an application (when each expires), the fee to extend, renew or reinstate one, and whether a 'final inspection only' permit is charged on the full job value: needed to cost the permits-to-finish-permits loop.
rows.says: An application expires if no permit is issued within 730 days of filing. An issued permit stays active for 365 days and each passed inspection extends it by another 365. A 180-day extension costs $415 each plus 20% of Plan Review Fees for an application and $228 each plus 10% of Building Permit Inspection Fees for a permit (2026 table). An expired permit cannot be extended and must be renewed. What a renewal or a 'final inspection only' permit costs, and whether it is charged on the full job value, is not in the 2026 tables; the 2024 fee ordinance listed restarting work that never began at 75% of current fee for the permit plus the full plan review fee. These time limits apply to applications filed on or after June 21, 2026 (Ordinance 259-25).

tables.how: Building Inspection's hourly inspection rate was $158.10 before the 2023 fee ordinance, which wrote in $181.82; the 2024 ordinance struck that out and wrote in $461 (+154%); the table effective July 12, 2026 prints $519, 3.3 times the figure of three years earlier. Most other fees are published for the current year only. Planning: a printed line is matched between the two schedules when its wording, with the amount removed, is identical and occurs once in each. tables.how: Across report years 2018 to 2025, San Francisco's median was 377 days from application to entitlement (rank 2 of 9, 1 being slowest), 254 days from entitlement to building permit (rank 3 of 9) and 561 days from permit to completion (rank 2 of 9). The slowest city on each measure was San Jose (433 days), San Jose (579) and Oakland (591). Oakland, Fresno reported the same date for application and entitlement on most projects, a difference in reporting rather than in speed. San Francisco reported 29,819 homes completed, 4.43 per 1,000 residents a year (rank 3 of 8 with a population figure, 1 being most). Rows are the projects each city reported to the State. Application to entitlement joins Table A to Table A2 on the city's own tracking number; entitlement to permit joins rows on the parcel number, taking the first permit on or after the entitlement; permit to completion joins on the tracking number. Medians cover intervals of 0 to 3,650 days ending in a report year, with at least 10 linked projects. Homes per 1,000 residents divide the units each city reported by its population, summed over the years with a population figure.
tables.limits: Each city fills in the dates by its own definitions, and the mix differs: most Los Angeles rows are accessory units and San Diego reports almost no entitlement dates. San Francisco files entitlements under a Planning record and permits under a building permit number, so only its parcel number links the two and few projects link. A parcel with two projects can be mis-joined. Projects that never reach the next stage are not counted, which flatters slow cities. The State department's 2023 review quoted averages on 2022 data, which are higher than these medians. Population comes from the Census for San Francisco and from the State Controller for the others; none is on disk for Berkeley. Unit counts are as each city reported them and a project can appear in more than one report year; the City's own count of net homes completed, used in the permit records screens, is lower.

tables.how: The 17 findings the rules analysis drew from 6 official documents on disk, and the 5 findings of City reviewers that the case lists under what is established. Each summary is this project's; the words in quotation marks are the document's.
tables.limits: These are the reviewers' findings, not this project's. The State review rests on research interviews and on data the City reported; departments' annual reports describe their own performance. The Mayor's 2025 permit reform directive and the 2018 directive on accessory dwelling units are saved only as scanned images without text and are not quoted. Reviews already in the project library (the Budget and Legislative Analyst, the Controller's public integrity reviews, the Civil Grand Jury) are reported in the permit records section, not repeated here.

tables.how: Every issued building permit with drawings filed 2012 to 2024 (179,746 permits) was ranked by days from filing to issue among like permits: the same permit type, review path (counter or full review, Fire-only, site permit, online filing, and the department's own priority flag), cost band and filing year. Cells under 30 permits were merged upward (three-year period, then paired cost bands) and 388 permits with no cell of 30 were dropped. A job is faster when it beat its cell's median; ties at the median are split in proportion so that chance gives exactly one half. Firms are tested with 40 or more jobs and at least 3 active years (5 or more jobs in the year); jobs for one lot filed on one day count once. Contractors are joined on their State licence number, other firms on the exact normalised name. With 1,157 firms tested, the usual one-in-twenty threshold would pass about 58 by luck alone, so the cut is set at 4.1 standard errors, where about 0.05 firms in the whole list would pass by luck. As a check on the arithmetic, the same permits dealt at random into 1,199 pretend firms put 5.8% beyond the usual threshold and 0 beyond the strict cut. Consistent means beyond that cut, on the same side of one half in at least three quarters of active years, and at least 55% (or at most 45%) overall. The last two columns repeat the comparison inside cells that also match the kind of work (keywords in the permit description) and the building's use. The list gives 1,081 of the 1,157 tested; the other 76 are individuals who are neither licensed nor registered and are counted, not named (9 of them consistently faster, 4 consistently slower). 60 meet the test for consistently faster and 93 for consistently slower; 517 differ at the usual one-in-twenty threshold. Connections are those of the reverse test: 348 tested firms have at least one and 809 have none.
tables.limits: Being fast is not wrongdoing. Speed has honest causes: complete drawings, repeat work in one building type, simple scopes inside a cost band, a specialty the cells do not capture (signs, fire alarms, mechanical work, office interiors), and experience. Where the difference does not survive the kind-of-work control it is most likely a specialty. The department's fee table prices a premium plan review (50% of Plan Review Fee plus $1,000), and its permit records carry a priority flag; one value of that flag is 'Premium' and the commonest others are 'ADU-State/Hybrid', 'Unit Legalization', 'Clean Energy', 'Housing-Aff'. The data dictionary does not define the values, so reading 'Premium' as the paid service is an inference. Permits are compared only with permits carrying the same kind of flag, and the share of each firm's jobs flagged Premium is shown. On 53% of full-review permits the first contractor was attached more than 60 days after filing, so a contractor's speed there may reflect its clients and designers. The records do not say whether a wait was the City's or the applicant's. Names typed differently on different permits are counted as different firms, which weakens the test and can split one firm into two rows. The file starts with 2012 filings. A group average hides individual firms in both directions, and connected firms are larger and do different work than unconnected ones, which the role-by-role comparison only partly removes. Permit consultants are hired for hard jobs, which would make them look slow, or for owners in a hurry, which would make them look fast; this test cannot tell which. Connections are exact name matches and are undercounted. A null result here does not clear any single firm, and a positive one does not accuse any. Each connection is an exact match of names between two records and is not confirmed: two firms can share a name, and an employer typed on a campaign form is the donor's own description.

tables.how: The speed test does not pick out the proven cases. Of 7 people and firms from the case files and the extra-scrutiny list with enough permits to test, 0 meet the test for consistently faster in the years the conduct covered. Rodrigo Santos (2012–2019): faster on 51% of 1,307 jobs, not distinguishable from like permits. SIA Consulting (2012–2021): faster on 42% of 347 jobs, somewhat slower: beyond the usual threshold only. 1 favourable result on another measure: SIA Consulting's full-review applications reached issue 83% of the time against 71% for like applications, enough to be listed in the screen 'Always approved, never held'. 1 result runs the other way: Harold Howell (Mercury Engineering Group, Inc.) is consistently slower on building permits (faster than like permits on only 36% of jobs). A method that cannot see the cases the courts have already proven cannot be read as clearing anyone it does not flag. The names are taken from the case files (the engineer and the design firm in the building-inspection case; the contractors in the Public Works case) and from Building Inspection's published extra-scrutiny list. Their permits are every building permit whose contact rows carry the person's name or the firm's name as the case file or the list gives it. The years are read from each case file's own timeline: from the first dated payment or gift to the last year those entries mention; for a listed person, every year up to the listing, with the years after it shown separately. The same like-for-like measures are then computed on those permits alone, with the same cuts as the screens above.
tables.limits: The proven conduct was about particular inspections, particular plan checks and money diverted from clients, none of which needs to show up as a faster average permit: a paid-for sign-off can change one job without moving an average, and a plan can be approved that should not be without being approved any sooner. A person is matched on the name typed on the permit, which can catch a namesake and miss a misspelling; each match here also carries the firm or the professional role the source gives. Days to issue is the only clock in the published data; who inspected what, and with what result, is not published at all. Being on the extra-scrutiny list or in a case file says nothing about any permit listed here. Being on the extra-scrutiny list is the department's own determination, published with a notice; what was proven in court is set out in the case file named in each row, and nothing in this list adds to it.
